RAM. Random-access memory. A type of volatile computer memory that allows fast read and write access to data in any order, regardless of location. It serves as the primary working memory for a computer's processor during active computation. Unlike permanent storage like hard drives and SSDs, RAM loses all data when power is cut, making it unsuitable for long-term storage but essential for real-time performance.

RAM is volatile memory. It requires continuous power to retain data; switching off the computer erases all contents instantly. The defining feature is random access: any memory location can be accessed in constant time, unlike sequential storage media such as tape, making it orders of magnitude faster. The processor loads programs and data into RAM during execution, reading and writing at nanosecond speeds. Modern systems have gigabytes of RAM, vastly more than CPU caches, which measure in megabytes, but less than permanent storage, which measures in terabytes.

There are two main types. Dynamic RAM requires periodic refresh to maintain charge. Static RAM holds data without refresh but is more expensive and power-hungry, used only for caches. An N-bit address bus can reference two to the power of N bytes. Thirty-two-bit systems address four gigabytes; sixty-four-bit systems address exabytes.

RAM latency—the time to first access—is about one hundred nanoseconds. Bandwidth, or data throughput, is tens of gigabytes per second. These represent a trade-off with frequency. RAM sits between the CPU and permanent storage in the memory hierarchy: slower than cache, much faster than storage. The CPU relies on RAM for all instruction and data storage during execution. Cache memory sits between CPU and RAM, holding frequently-accessed data to reduce latency. Virtual memory extends effective memory by swapping RAM contents to disk when capacity is exceeded. The motherboard physically hosts RAM chips, and bus bandwidth limits RAM speed. RAM is the canonical example of the trade-off between volatile and non-volatile storage: it trades permanence for speed.
